Hey, I'm Séverin.

I'm a repeat founder and product builder.
I've been building on language models since GPT-3's davinci.

I don't make models. Models learn in training. The software I build learns at runtime.

What I'm working on

Since the davinci days, one obsession: the most value from a model, with the fewest errors, from the fewest tokens. The answer I keep arriving at is that an agent's work shouldn't evaporate when the context window closes. Every action should leave behind a runnable, tested artifact that the next agent starts from — so the system gets better by being used, not by waiting for a bigger model. Three lines of work follow from that, all under Creative Robots, the company I've been running since 2021.

I

Capture what works, as code.

Ask an agent to list your last ten emails and it rewrites the integration from scratch, every time, and succeeds maybe 30–60% of the time. The fix isn't a smarter model. It's remembering what worked — as a file that runs, has tests, and can be shared with every other agent. Muscle memory, in software.

OpenIntegrations — formerly skills.dev
prototype

A registry of every API action in the world — ~7.9k providers, ~18.7k actions — each with a schema, the TypeScript that runs it, the gotchas, and a run button. Call an action nobody has implemented and an agent writes and tests it mid-request; the first call takes a minute, every call after takes milliseconds, for everyone. Reliability is earned, not asserted: documented → developed → tested → reliable, graded hourly from real runs, and every proposed change is replayed against every benchmark before it can land.

The first version, skills.dev (~288K LOC), predated Agent Skills. Anthropic shipping them is the clearest validation the idea has had; the domain has since gone to Vercel, and the work is being rebuilt as this.

Slices
launching soon

The same idea for a codebase. Every registry hands you a table and wishes you luck — but a table is a view onto a collection, and a collection means auth, an audit trail, a database and a route that filters what each user may see. One shadcn-compatible command writes all six into your repo, and it stays yours. 27 patterns, 6 families, 8 service contracts with 15 interchangeable implementations, all held to one conformance suite. It's a waste to burn a million tokens every time you need a sign-in screen.

Layouts.dev — where it started
2021 — 2025

Artifacts are only reusable if a model can be trusted to edit them. So: a DSL up to 10× terser than React, compiling one parse tree to Next.js and Expo, whose grammar cannot express a side effect or an infinite loop — validation is parsing, not linting. Built in 2021 because davinci was hopeless at React; turned out to be better DX for designers too. 256 visual-test fixtures keep web and native output in step.

II

If the artifact is code, the software can rewrite itself.

Once what an agent learns is stored as code, nothing stops the system from changing its own tools, its own interface, or its own source. These are the experiments in how far that goes.

protean

An agent whose working directory is its own source. Anything it drops in ~/tools/ becomes a tool on the next turn — so “I don't have a camera” is solved by writing one. It edits its own code, commits, and restarts into the new version; it migrates to other machines over P2P, carrying its state on a CRDT. The only constraint left is budget, which is why it needs a supervisor and a crash ladder that walks back through git history until it boots again — because it can and does brick itself.

Try — create an agent, run the command on your own machine, then ask it to photograph you by building the tool first, to spawn itself a server with the AWS CLI, or to spread to a Raspberry Pi on your network.

ux-morph
live

Interfaces are authored once, by the vendor, for an imaginary average user. Mark a Next.js page use morph and each signed-in user gets their own compiled copy: they describe a change in plain language, it is typechecked, and the site rebuilds around them. Feedback becoming interface. An experiment, not a product.

Try — pick any persona, then ask it to “Make this look like Win95”.

open-widgets
live

Describe a component, get a real one — installed, typechecked and bundled in a sandbox, embeddable anywhere behind one tag. The generated code never runs on your page. The smallest possible unit of “a description became an artifact”.

III

A loop that stops for a human isn't a loop.

None of the above compounds if the agent has to wake someone up to sign in, fetch a key, or click through a console. Every layer of the cloud checks for a human. These are the layers that don't — identity, credentials, resources — and the place where they all get tested at once.

Interagentic — identity
beta

A machine signs a token with its own key and exchanges it for a ten-minute one addressed to a single service. That service does one JWKS check and learns which machine is calling, whether a human stands behind it, who that human is — a different pseudonym at every service — and what they allowed. Identity is a keypair, not a name: nothing to register, nothing to sign up for at 3am.

Keychains — credentials
live

Give the agent the keys, not the kingdom. It sends a {{OAUTH2_TOKEN}} placeholder; the proxy resolves the provider, injects the real token, forwards, and streams the response back. The secret never enters the context window, so a prompt injection has nothing to steal. Scope inference across 6,000+ APIs from ~1.88M lines of provider docs; pay-per-call over x402 so an agent can use an API with no account at all.

ExtraOrbital — resources
beta

npx extraorbital provision . reads the project, finds the environment variables the code references, creates the real Mongo cluster, S3 bucket, Redis and model keys, and writes them back to .env.local. No console, no card. Every provision is idempotent and takes a lease first, so an agent can run it in a retry loop, in CI, on restart, and never double-spend.

BotParty — the test
live

Agents forming teams to build an entire company, with their own computers, Slack, Trello and Notion, on top of the three layers above. What do agents do when nobody is prompting them, and where does the output stop being trustworthy?

How I got here

Creative Robots
2021 — now

I built my first vibe-coding product before ChatGPT, when models didn't reliably know how to emit valid JSON. It churned too much to trust — the output evaporated as fast as it was generated — so I spent the two years after that on rail-coding: a grammar the model can't get wrong, and features instead of components as the unit of reuse. That became Layouts.dev, then Slices.

The agent work followed from the same instinct one level up: if a model's output shouldn't evaporate, neither should what an agent learns. Everything above is the same company, still going.
